n: Now settled in a cedar palace, David is troubled that the ark of God still sits in a tent. He tells Nathan the prophet he wants to build God a house.

f.g: In a tent, under fabric hangings.

n: Nathan quickly approves, assuming God will bless David’s good intentions. Even prophets sometimes speak from their own judgment before receiving revelation.

f.w: Do all that is in thine heart
f.g: Nathan’s personal opinion, which the Lord soon corrects.

n: That same night God speaks to Nathan with a different message.

f.w: the word of God came to Nathan

n: God tells David he is not the one to build the temple. 1 Chronicles 22:8 later explains that David had shed much blood in war.

f.w: Thou shalt not build me an house

n: God reminds David that since the Exodus He has lived among His people in a moving tent. He has always gone where they went.
God never asked any leader for a cedar house. A temple is a gift God accepts on His terms, not something He needs.
The Lord reminds David where he came from: a shepherd boy taken from the sheep pens to lead God’s people.
God has been with David everywhere, defeated his enemies, and made his name great—promises that echo God’s covenant with Abraham.
God promises to give Israel a secure home where they will be “planted” and no longer oppressed by wicked people.
Then the great reversal: David wanted to build God a house, but God will build David a “house”—a lasting dynasty. It is a beautiful play on the word “house.”

f.w: the LORD will build thee an house
f.g: “House” here means a royal family line, not a building.

n: After David dies, God will raise up one of his sons and establish his kingdom.
This son will build God’s house, and God will establish his throne forever. Solomon built the temple, but the “forever” throne finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.

f.w: I will stablish his throne for ever

n: God will be a Father to David’s son and never withdraw His covenant love as He did from Saul. Hebrews applies this verse to Christ, the Son of God.

f.w: I will be his father, and he shall be my son

n: God will set David’s son over “mine house and… my kingdom”—showing that Israel’s kingdom is really God’s kingdom. Where 2 Samuel says “thy kingdom,” Chronicles stresses God’s ownership.

f.w: in mine house and in my kingdom

n: Nathan faithfully delivers the whole revelation to David.

f.g: According to the revelation God gave him.

n: David goes in and sits before the Lord, overwhelmed: “Who am I…?” His humility is the right response to God’s grace.

f.w: Who am I, O LORD God

n: David marvels that God, not content with present blessings, has promised his family a future far beyond his lifetime.

f.g: A person of high rank or honor.

n: David is lost for words: what more can I say? You know me.
David acknowledges that God did all this from His own heart and goodness, not because David earned it.

f.g: By Your own will and gracious purpose.

n: There is no one like the Lord and no God besides Him.
David praises God for redeeming Israel from Egypt and making them His people—a unique nation shaped by God’s mighty acts.

f.g: To buy back or rescue; used of the Exodus and, ultimately, of Christ’s redemption.

n: God made Israel His own people forever and became their God—the heart of the covenant.
David asks God to do exactly as He promised. Good prayers often take God at His word.
David’s deepest desire is that God’s name, not his own, be honored forever through this covenant.

f.w: that thy name may be magnified for ever

n: Because God has made this promise, David finds the courage to pray.

f.w: found in his heart to pray
f.g: Found the courage or desire to pray.

n: David affirms that the Lord is God and has promised this good thing.
David closes by asking God to bless his house forever, confident that whatever God blesses stays blessed.

f.w: thou blessest, O LORD, and it shall be blessed for ever
